prompt:
Write 11 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a low-speed head-on collision claim, in time order. Injury: neck and back strain. The claimant is represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1148; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The reported injury matches the kind and force of the crash well.
- Treatment followed a usual course and tapered off as the patient improved.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Photos confirm some details, but there are no independent witnesses.
- It is not clear whether all of the damage came from this impact.
- The claimant told the same account in every conversation.
- The police and witnesses confirm the claimant was in the vehicle.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- Nothing suggests the damage happened before the coverage started.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: The claim was reported by the insured's representing attorney after a low-speed head-on collision, and the adjuster opened a file and requested the police report and initial photographs.

Entry 2: The police report confirms the claimant was in the vehicle at the time of the collision, and the driver is named on the policy in force on the loss date.

Entry 3: Scene photographs show the front-end damage and confirm several details of the impact, but no independent witnesses have come forward to describe how the collision happened.

Entry 4: Reviewing the vehicle file, no prior damage to the vehicle is known, and nothing in the records suggests the damage occurred before the coverage period began.

Entry 5: The claimant reports neck and back strain and has described the same account in every conversation so far, with the injury pattern appearing consistent with the kind and force of this crash.

Entry 6: The claimant's medical records show no earlier injury to the same body area, and the treatment so far has followed a usual course that has tapered off as the claimant improved.

Entry 7: Repair estimates have been reviewed, but it is not yet clear whether all of the listed damage came from this impact, so the appraiser has been asked to inspect the vehicle again.

Entry 8: Counsel for the claimant confirmed by letter that the claimant will provide the treatment records and wage information requested in the earlier correspondence.

Entry 9: The adjuster spoke with the treating provider's office, which confirmed the visit dates and the course of care, and noted that the claimant's account of symptoms has stayed consistent across each visit.

Entry 10: Pending receipt of the appraiser's supplemental report, the adjuster is reviewing whether the damage listing needs to be separated by cause before any settlement offer is made.

Entry 11: The file remains open while the supplemental appraisal and outstanding records are collected, and the adjuster will update the reserve once those items are received.
